questions.statement: What is a topic sentence?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: A sentence that states the main idea of a paragraph
options.feedback: The topic sentence carries the paragraph's central idea for the reader.

options.text: The last sentence of a paragraph, always
options.feedback: A topic sentence usually comes first, though it can appear at the end.

options.text: A sentence that contains the longest word
options.feedback: Nothing in the definition depends on the length of the words used.

options.text: A question that the paragraph answers
options.feedback: A topic sentence states an idea; it does not need to be a question.

questions.explanation: A topic sentence states the main idea of a paragraph and tells the reader what that paragraph is about.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of walking to school.
questions.context: A paragraph writing exercise in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: My neighbour walks to school every single day without fail.
options.feedback: This is a narrow anecdote about one person, too specific to govern a whole paragraph.

options.text: Walking to school has real benefits for health and the environment.
options.feedback: The sentence names the subject and the two fields it will cover, which the rest can develop.

options.text: Yesterday afternoon was sunny and warm.
options.feedback: The sentence is about the weather and would lead the paragraph in the wrong direction.

options.text: Buses are common in cities.
options.feedback: This introduces a different subject, and 'common' adds nothing that can be explained.

questions.explanation: A good topic sentence announces the subject of the paragraph in general terms and can be developed into several supporting sentences.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is a suitable supporting sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of walking to school?
questions.context: A paragraph writing task in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The sky above the road was blue that morning.
options.feedback: A description of the weather adds nothing to the benefits being developed.

options.text: Paragraphs are made of several sentences.
options.feedback: That is a definition of a paragraph and does not support the stated topic.

options.text: Walking adds gentle exercise without any need for a gym membership.
options.feedback: The sentence expands the health benefit named in the topic sentence.

options.text: Some people prefer to walk very slowly.
options.feedback: The speed of walking is not one of the benefits the paragraph set out to explain.

questions.explanation: A supporting sentence develops one of the ideas announced by the topic sentence and explains it further.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a concluding sentence in a paragraph?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To introduce an entirely new topic for the next paragraph
options.feedback: New topics belong in a new paragraph, usually with a clear link.

options.text: To repeat the title word for no reason at all
options.feedback: A conclusion must add meaning, not merely echo a word from the title.

options.text: To ask the reader a question they cannot answer
options.feedback: An unanswerable question adds confusion rather than closing the argument.

options.text: To close the paragraph by summarising its main point
options.feedback: The last sentence wraps up what the paragraph has developed.

questions.explanation: A concluding sentence closes the paragraph by summarising its idea or leaving the reader with a final thought on the topic.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best concluding sentence for a paragraph about why libraries matter.
questions.context: A paragraph writing exercise in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: The word library begins with the letter l and has seven letters.
options.feedback: Counting letters adds nothing to the argument about why libraries matter.

options.text: There are no other places with books in the city.
options.feedback: The claim is false and would damage the paragraph's credibility.

options.text: Paragraphs should always end with a question.
options.feedback: That is a rule that is not true and does not suit this paragraph.

options.text: For all their quiet rooms and long shelves, libraries remain open to anyone who wants to learn.
options.feedback: The sentence gathers the ideas and closes with a broader statement about access.

questions.explanation: A strong conclusion pulls the paragraph's points together and restates their importance in a fresh way.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence belongs in the body of a paragraph rather than in its conclusion?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: In short, libraries remain valuable to the whole community.
options.feedback: The phrase 'in short' marks a summary, which belongs in a conclusion.

options.text: To sum up, access to books should be treated as a public good.
options.feedback: The phrase 'to sum up' signals a closing summary of the argument.

options.text: For example, the branch library lends materials to people who have no internet at home.
options.feedback: The sentence gives a concrete example that develops the idea, which is the work of the body.

options.text: All in all, these places matter more than ever before.
options.feedback: The expression 'all in all' marks a wrap-up, so this is a concluding sentence.

questions.explanation: Body sentences develop the main idea with details and examples, while a conclusion summarises what has already been developed.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why should a paragraph contain only one main idea?
questions.context: A writing skills lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Because paragraphs must always be exactly five sentences long
options.feedback: A paragraph has no fixed length; the number of sentences depends on the idea.

options.text: So that the paragraph stays focused and easy to follow
options.feedback: One idea per paragraph gives the reader a clear thread through the text.

options.text: Because teachers reduce the marks for long paragraphs
options.feedback: Marks depend on content and accuracy, not on how long a paragraph is.

options.text: Because shorter paragraphs use less ink when printed
options.feedback: Practical printing costs are not the reason writers organise paragraphs as they do.

questions.explanation: A single idea keeps the paragraph focused, so the reader can follow the argument without the writer jumping between subjects.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best way to order ideas in a body paragraph.
questions.context: A paragraph writing exercise in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: From the main point to the supporting examples that explain it
options.feedback: Starting with the general idea and following with details gives the reader a clear structure.

options.text: From the most surprising detail to the main point at the end
options.feedback: Leaving the main idea to the end can leave the reader unsure what the paragraph was for.

options.text: In random order, because each idea stands on its own
options.feedback: Random order hides the connection between the point and its examples.

options.text: In strict chronological order of when you thought of them
options.feedback: The order in which ideas come to mind is not the order in which they explain each other.

questions.explanation: Ideas are usually arranged from the most general or important point to the supporting details, which keeps the reader oriented.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which transition helps a reader follow a contrast between two ideas?
questions.context: A writing lesson in a school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Moreover,
options.feedback: 'Moreover' adds a further supporting point rather than an opposing one.

options.text: However,
options.feedback: The word signals that the following sentence will oppose what came before.

options.text: For example,
options.feedback: That phrase introduces an illustration of the previous point.

options.text: In other words,
options.feedback: That phrase restates the same idea in different words.

questions.explanation: A contrast transition signals that the next idea opposes the previous one, and examples are 'however', 'in contrast' or 'on the other hand'.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is a topic sentence for a paragraph about the reasons people volunteer?
questions.context: A paragraph planning task in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Maria volunteers at the library on Tuesdays and Fridays.
options.feedback: One person's routine is too narrow to serve as the idea of a whole paragraph.

options.text: Volunteering is something.
options.feedback: The statement is too vague to be developed, and it names no idea at all.

options.text: I do not volunteer at all myself.
options.feedback: That is a personal remark, not an idea about why other people volunteer.

options.text: People volunteer for a variety of reasons.
options.feedback: The sentence announces the topic without committing to a single narrow example, leaving room to develop it.

questions.explanation: A topic sentence must name the subject of the paragraph and be broad enough to be explained by several following sentences.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best concluding sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of walking to school.
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Some people also drive to school when the weather is cold.
options.feedback: The sentence adds a new point rather than closing the paragraph.

options.text: Walking is a form of movement that people do every day.
options.feedback: The sentence is a definition, which restates nothing the paragraph developed.

options.text: For all its effort, walking to school turns out to benefit both health and the local air.
options.feedback: It gathers the two points into a final judgement about their combined value.

options.text: The number of cars on the road was counted last year.
options.feedback: The statistic is a new detail and does not summarise the argument.

questions.explanation: A conclusion must wrap up the points the paragraph developed and restate their significance without introducing new material.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would make the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the effects of noise on study?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Noise in a study space reduces concentration and lowers the quality of work produced.
options.feedback: It states the subject and a claim that details about concentration and work can develop.

options.text: The reading room has fifty seats and four windows.
options.feedback: It gives the setting's measurements rather than a claim about the effects of noise.

options.text: The window nearest the road was replaced last spring.
options.feedback: The sentence gives a maintenance detail that develops no argument at all.

options.text: Some students wear headphones while they work.
options.feedback: The observation concerns coping behaviour, not the paragraph's stated topic.

questions.explanation: A topic sentence must name the subject and offer a claim that the following sentences can support with evidence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which connector should introduce the second supporting sentence in a paragraph about public transport?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: For instance,
options.feedback: The additive connector introduces a further point that supports the same idea.

options.text: Nevertheless,
options.feedback: The word introduces an alternative condition, not a second supporting detail.

options.text: Otherwise,
options.feedback: The word marks a substitution, which does not fit an additional supporting point.

options.text: Furthermore,
options.feedback: A contrastive connector would signal an opposing point instead of an additional one.

questions.explanation: A connector shows the reader how the new sentence relates to the previous one, and an additive connector adds to the point already made.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How should a writer choose which details to include in a paragraph?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: By including every fact that comes to mind about the topic
options.feedback: Extra facts dilute the paragraph and hide the main point from the reader.

options.text: By keeping only those that support the topic sentence
options.feedback: Relevance to the stated idea is the criterion for including a detail.

options.text: By choosing the shortest details available
options.feedback: Brevity alone does not make a detail relevant to the topic sentence.

options.text: By adding details that contradict the topic sentence
options.feedback: A contradiction would confuse the reader instead of developing the idea.

questions.explanation: Only details that explain or prove the topic sentence belong in the paragraph; the rest distract from it.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Complete the paragraph: 'Volunteering takes time and sometimes involves real expense. ___ it also builds skills that employers value.'
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: However, it
options.feedback: 'However' introduces a contrast between the cost and the benefit, which the sentence then develops.

options.text: Because of that, it
options.feedback: A causal connector would claim the benefit is the result of the cost, which is not the relationship.

options.text: In short, it
options.feedback: The phrase marks a summary and belongs at the end of the paragraph.

options.text: In other words, it
options.feedback: The phrase restates the same idea in different words rather than adding a new one.

questions.explanation: The second clause adds a benefit to the costs already listed, so an additive connector is the right choice.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the purpose of a concluding sentence that begins with 'In conclusion'?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: To introduce a completely new topic
options.feedback: A new topic would normally begin a new paragraph with its own topic sentence.

options.text: To repeat an earlier sentence word for word
options.feedback: Copying wording rather than summarising adds no value to the reader.

options.text: To summarise the main point of the paragraph
options.feedback: The phrase signals the closing summary the reader should retain.

options.text: To ask the reader to write the conclusion
options.feedback: The paragraph belongs to the writer, not to the reader.

questions.explanation: The phrase announces that the paragraph is ending and that the writer is about to summarise what has been developed.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the paragraph in which every sentence serves the same main idea.
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: School gardens are pleasant. The weather last week was warm. Some students prefer novels to films. Lunch is served at one o'clock.
options.feedback: The sentences move between unrelated subjects and serve no single idea.

options.text: School gardens give students a practical lesson in care. They learn to prepare soil and to notice when a plant is failing. Several classes now sell what they grow to raise money.
options.feedback: Each sentence develops the idea of what the garden teaches and what results from it.

options.text: School gardens need funding, as explained in the paragraph above, which is not really present.
options.feedback: The paragraph refers to an explanation it never provides, so it develops nothing.

options.text: Nobody knows why gardens exist, although many are built and are used every day.
options.feedback: The opening and the closing contradict each other and no idea is developed.

questions.explanation: A coherent paragraph is one in which each sentence develops the single idea stated in the topic sentence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is a topic sentence usually placed at the beginning of a paragraph?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: So the reader knows the point before the supporting details begin
options.feedback: An early statement of the idea gives the reader a frame for everything after it.

options.text: So the paragraph always begins with the longest sentence
options.feedback: Position has nothing to do with the length of the sentences involved.

options.text: Because English grammar forbids the topic sentence elsewhere
options.feedback: The topic sentence can also appear at the end; it is not forbidden there.

options.text: Because supporting details cannot follow a statement of the idea
options.feedback: Details follow the topic sentence all the time, which is the normal pattern.

questions.explanation: Placing the main idea first tells the reader what the paragraph is about before the supporting detail begins.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the best supporting detail for the topic sentence 'Regular reading improves writing skills'.
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: Many people enjoy reading books in a quiet room.
options.feedback: The sentence is a general statement of preference rather than evidence for the claim.

options.text: Reading is a hobby that some families share together.
options.feedback: The sentence discusses the activity socially and does not support the claim about writing.

options.text: Students who read every week produced longer and better organised essays in the same term.
options.feedback: The detail offers concrete evidence that connects the reading habit to the writing skill.

options.text: Some bookshops open earlier on Saturdays than on weekdays.
options.feedback: The detail is about shop hours and has no bearing on writing skills at all.

questions.explanation: A supporting detail must provide evidence or an example for the claim in the topic sentence.
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What should a writer do to make a paragraph's ending feel purposeful?
questions.context: A paragraph writing lesson in a secondary school in San Salvador, SV.

options.text: End with a question that the paragraph never prepared the reader for
options.feedback: An unexpected question leaves the reader puzzled rather than satisfied.

options.text: End with a fact about a completely unrelated subject
options.feedback: An unrelated final sentence disconnects the ending from the rest of the paragraph.

options.text: End abruptly with a single word and no full sentence
options.feedback: An abrupt fragment gives the reader no sense of closure at all.

options.text: End with a sentence that follows from the paragraph's own points
options.feedback: A closing derived from the earlier detail gives the paragraph logical completeness.

questions.explanation: An ending that follows from what came before it closes the paragraph logically and signals to the reader that it is finished.
questions.subject: ingles
